sections.category: Sakana's Fugu Ultra orchestration model meets its first independent reality check: benchmark-parity claims collide with 30-minute coding runs

bullets.body: Sakana AI's new Fugu, launched June 22 and offered as a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint, is itself a language model trained to route, delegate, verify, and synthesize across a swappable pool of frontier LLMs, including recursive calls to instances of itself; the design builds on two ICLR 2026 papers, TRINITY (an evolved lightweight coordinator) and Conductor (reinforcement-learned natural-language orchestration), and the top-tier Fugu Ultra tier is pitched as matching Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos on Sakana's own published coding, scientific, and reasoning tables without training a frontier model from scratch. The fresh development this cycle is the first independent pushback landing within 48 hours of launch: Wharton's Ethan Mollick ran Fugu Ultra on his standard shader and interactive-scene coding tests and reported that it is "incredibly slow" with typical runs taking about 30 minutes rather than minutes, and that output was "fine" but did not match Fable in practice, so the published parity scores have not been independently reproduced. The signal is that learned multi-model orchestration can approach frontier quality on paper while paying a steep latency tax that benchmark tables do not surface, which is exactly the gap a router-as-a-model architecture has to close to be usable. sections.category: Micron joins Anthropic's Series H, putting all three HBM makers inside one frontier lab's memory supply chain

bullets.body: Micron and Anthropic announced a strategic partnership on June 22 that bundles four pieces: a memory-and-storage co-design effort targeting performance, energy efficiency, and token economics; a multi-year supply allocation spanning HBM, DRAM, and SSDs from Micron's data-center portfolio; an internal Claude rollout across Micron's engineering, manufacturing, and enterprise functions; and a strategic equity investment by Micron in Anthropic's Series H. The round itself, a $65 billion raise at a roughly $965 billion post-money valuation, closed May 28, but the new fact is Micron's entry, which means all three global HBM suppliers, Micron alongside Samsung and SK Hynix, are now Series H participants and Anthropic infrastructure partners, a coupling no other frontier lab currently holds. Neither the supply-agreement value nor Micron's investment size was disclosed, so any specific dollar figure circulating is unconfirmed. The structural read is that frontier labs are locking up high-bandwidth-memory capacity through equity, not just purchase orders, ahead of expected Q4 2026 public listings, tightening the link between AI-model roadmaps and the memory-fabrication supply chain. sections.category: Physical AI lands on the factory floor at Automate 2026: Cobot's second-generation Proxie ships on-robot inference with a production track record

bullets.body: Collaborative Robotics unveiled its second-generation Proxie on June 22 at Automate 2026, framing it as a general-purpose mobile collaborative robot that identifies the work to be done and does it with zero software integration and no human dispatcher. The fresh artifact is that Gen 2 moves task inference fully on-robot, with no cloud dependency for core execution, paired with a ScoutSense sensor stack that perceives the workspace at human eye level, plans and sequences the work, and audibly announces each action; the robot moves carts up to 1,500 pounds, lifts up to 200 pounds vertically, and is offered starting at $5,000 per month. Cobot anchored the launch on a concrete production record from the first generation: 12,627 hours logged in real operations, over 40 million pounds of material moved, and more than 17 million human steps saved across hospitals, manufacturing, and logistics on 16-hour daily shifts. The launch sits inside the broader Automate 2026 show (June 22-25, McCormick Place), whose dominant theme is physical AI, robots trained by demonstration rather than explicit programming, with a first-time NVIDIA-sponsored Humanoid Robot Pavilion hosting more than 20 humanoid platforms, marking the industry's shift from humanoid research to commercial deployment. sections.category: AI events to plan around now: the offensive-security and dev-conference tracks open this week, with the chip and security calendar running into the fall

bullets.body: The forward calendar across all three sub-tracks, with the soonest items days away (the Confidential Computing Summit, June 23-24 at the SF Mint, closes today and drops off the forward list). AI-security: AI Tinkerers San Francisco hosts an Offensive Security Demo Night on June 25 with live autonomous-pentesting-agent demos backed by sponsor XBOW; further out, Black Hat USA's AI Summit runs August 1-6 in Las Vegas alongside DEF CON's AI Village, SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit follows August 11-12 at Half Moon Bay, OWASP Global AppSec USA is November 5-6 in San Francisco, and Zenity's AI Agent Security Summit series stays on the watch list. Mainstream dev/data: Snowflake runs a virtual Dev Day on June 25 (two luminary talks plus a hands-on agentic-AI lab), the AI Engineer World's Fair takes over Moscone West with main programming June 29 through July 2 (optional New Engineer Orientation June 28), preceded by the official AIE World's Fair Hackathon with Cerebral Valley on June 27-28, and GitHub Universe returns October 28-29 with AWS re:Invent November 30 to December 4 in Las Vegas. AI-chip/hardware: Automate 2026 is running now (June 22-25, McCormick Place) with a first-time NVIDIA-sponsored Humanoid Robot Pavilion and a Humanoid Robot Forum on June 23-24; AMD's Advancing AI 2026 is set for July 22-23 at Moscone (Instinct MI400-series focus expected, keynote July 23), Hot Chips 2026 runs August 23-25 at Stanford, and the AI Infra Summit is September 15-17 at the Santa Clara Convention Center.
